headline: A trading account that loses 50% needs a 100% gain just to get back to where it started. A loss and the gain that repairs it are never the same size.

note.line1: A trading account that loses 50% needs a 100% gain just to get back to where it started.
note.line2: A loss and the gain that repairs it are never the same size.
note.caption: After a drawdown, the next gain is earned on a smaller balance. An account that falls from 100 to 50 has to double to return to 100. The gain needed to recover a loss d is d / (1 − d): 11.1% after a 10% loss, 25% after a 20% loss, 100% after a 50% loss. This is why the depth of a drawdown matters more than it first appears.

headline: Is a trading system that wins 90% of its trades always profitable?
topic: trading questions / win rate and expectancy

note.question: Is a trading system that wins 90% of its trades always profitable?
note.caption: No. What a system earns per trade is its expectancy: the win rate times the average win, minus the loss rate times the average loss. A system that wins 90% of the time with an average gain of 1 and an average loss of 10 earns 0.9 × 1 − 0.1 × 10 = −0.1 per trade. Over 100 trades that is 90 wins worth +90 and 10 losses worth −100, a net result of −10. A win rate says how often a system is right, not how much it makes.
note.topic: trading questions / win rate and expectancy

headline: Survivorship bias: The error of judging past market returns only from the funds, stocks or strategies that still exist today, leaving out those that closed or failed. The losers are missing from the data, so the past looks better than it was.

note.text: The error of judging past market returns only from the funds, stocks or strategies that still exist today, leaving out those that closed or failed.
note.line2: The losers are missing from the data, so the past looks better than it was.
note.caption: Funds that perform poorly are more likely to be closed or merged, and companies that fail drop out of an index. A study that keeps only the survivors therefore overstates the average return that was actually available at the time. The same trap appears in trading research when a strategy is tested only on the stocks that make up an index today. A fair test includes everything that existed on each date, including what later disappeared.

headline: Ten losing trades in a row, risking 2% each: −18.3%. Not 20%. Each loss is 2% of a balance that has already shrunk. 0.98 to the power of ten is 0.817.
topic: risk and position sizing / consecutive losses

note.label: Ten losing trades in a row, risking 2% each
note.line1: Not 20%. Each loss is 2% of a balance that has already shrunk.
note.line2: 0.98 to the power of ten is 0.817.
note.caption: When a trader risks a fixed fraction of the current balance, each loss is taken from a smaller amount than the one before. After ten losses of 2% the account keeps 0.98 to the power of ten, about 81.7% of where it started, so the total loss is about 18.3% rather than 20%. Losses expressed as percentages of a changing balance multiply rather than add. The same arithmetic works in the other direction for gains.
note.topic: risk and position sizing / consecutive losses

headline: Myth: After five losing trades in a row, a winning trade is due. Fact: If trades are independent, the chance of a win on the next trade is the same as before the streak.

note.myth: After five losing trades in a row, a winning trade is due.
note.fact: If trades are independent, the chance of a win on the next trade is the same as before the streak.
note.caption: Expecting a reversal after a run of losses is known as the gambler's fallacy. When the outcome of each trade does not depend on the ones before it, a streak carries no information about the next result. A system that wins 40% of its trades still has a 40% chance of winning the sixth trade after five losses. Over many trades the overall ratio moves towards the true win rate because new trades dilute the streak, not because past losses are paid back.
